summary: Explains how filters that follow RFC 1858 can still be fooled by a variant of the tiny fragment attack, and recommends a fix. The attack hides important header information by splitting packets into very small pieces.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo explains how overlapping IP fragments can alter a TCP header after a filter has inspected a different fragment. It recommends dropping certain incomplete TCP fragments before reassembly.

subtitle: A correction for a tiny overlapping fragment attack that can bypass some filters.

tldr.problem: RFC 1858's Indirect Method can miss a combination of tiny and overlapping fragments that changes a TCP destination port.
tldr.mechanism: The memo recommends dropping TCP fragments with offset zero that contain less than a complete header, as well as fragments with offset one.
tldr.outcome: The additional check addresses the variant described here and updates RFC 1858.

today: RFC 3128 is Informational and updates RFC 1858. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 3128.

sections.title: The Indirect Method's Weakness
sections.content:
RFC 1858 describes attacks on firewalls that filter fragmented packets. This memo says its Indirect Method is vulnerable to a combination of the Tiny Fragment Attack and the Overlapping Fragment Attack.

The issue applies where rules allow incoming connections to a machine while other ports on that host should accept only outgoing connections. The memo says only the initial connection message needs to be fragmented; later traffic on the established connection is legal.
sections.plainLanguage: A filter can inspect one fragment, while the destination later combines it with an overlapping fragment that changes the TCP header. This memo describes that gap.

sections.title: The Three-Fragment Attack
sections.content:
The example uses three fragments. Fragment 1 has offset zero and length at least 16, so it includes a complete header and may describe a permitted incoming connection. Fragment 2 also has offset zero but is only 8 bytes long; it carries port numbers and a sequence number, and may replace the destination port with one that should not accept incoming connections.

Fragment 3 has offset at least 2 and completes the message. Depending on how the destination reassembles fragments, fragment 2 may overwrite fragment 1 and change the apparent connection to Telnet on port 23.
sections.plainLanguage: The first fragment can look permitted. A second, shorter fragment can overlap it and change the destination port when the fragments are reassembled.

sections.title: Why the Existing Test Misses It
sections.content:
The Indirect Method rejects packets with fragment offset 1. None of the fragments in this attack has offset 1, so that test does not reject them.

The method assumed that moving interesting header fields out of an offset-zero fragment requires an offset-one fragment. The RFC explains that a forged 8-byte offset-zero fragment does not have to follow that assumption.
sections.plainLanguage: The existing test looks for a fragment with offset one. This attack uses offset-zero fragments instead, so the test does not catch it.

sections.title: Countermeasures
sections.content:
In addition to dropping TCP fragments with offset one, the memo says filters must drop offset-zero TCP fragments that contain less than a complete transport header. It gives the rule using TRANSPORTLEN < tmin for the incomplete-header test.

The Security Considerations section says the memo is concerned entirely with security implications of filtering fragmented IP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Filters should also drop offset-zero TCP fragments that are too short to contain a complete header. The memo gives this as an additional check to the offset-one rule.

references.text: Ziemba, G., Reed, D. and P. Traina, "Security Considerations for IP Fragment Filtering", RFC 1858, October 1995.
